We hosted a 𝗥𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗼𝗻 𝗕𝗶𝗼-𝗔𝗜: 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘆-𝗔𝗰𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗺𝗶𝗮 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻, in collaboration with Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) Hyderabad, the Institute of genomics and integrative biology (CSIR) and the BRIC - Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics (CDFD).

Dr. Satya Prakash Dash, Prof. Ullas Kolthur and Dr. Anand Anandkumar initiated the session. This was followed by speakers from academia, startups and industry sharing their expertise, with the aim of identifying, generating and building real collaborations and partnerships that are problem specific.

The discussion highlighted the need for good-quality datasets that are specific to our population and geography; compute that is still too slow for the work being asked of it; and the design-build-test-learn cycle — keeping the lab inside the loop, so that every computational prediction meets an experiment and every experimental result improves the next model. Alongside this came the harder question of validation, and what metrics we should be using to build and judge these algorithms in the first place.

The emphasis was on building shared, open capability rather than parallel private efforts.

Our thanks to every speaker and participant for their time and open conversation.

Researchers at IIT Delhi have developed a scalable, atomically thin 𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶-𝘀𝗰𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵 𝗰𝗼𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗴𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘀 that improves scratch resistance without hindering the optical transparency of the glass.

The work was conducted under the guidance of 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗳. Nitya Nand Gosvami and 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗳. N M Anoop Krishnan 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗜𝗜𝗧 𝗗𝗲𝗹𝗵𝗶, along with 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗳. Viswanath Balakrishnan 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗜𝗜𝗧 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶.

A two-dimensional tungsten disulfide (WS₂) film is coated directly on the glass surface in a single-step chemical vapour deposition process. 

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘀:
 • Nanoscale friction reduced by ~95% against a diamond probe (AFM scratch testing)
 • Severe plowing wear suppressed, even with a single monolayer
 • Uniform growth demonstrated over 0.25 m²
 
With applications spanning electronics, architectural glazing, automotive glazing and aerospace glass, this technology opens new possibilities for improving the durability of glass surfaces without compromising their optical performance.

Phool asked a question nobody else had asked: what can we do with flower waste?

The science. The first answer was flowercycling, turning temple flowers into incense. A good answer, and a tempting place to stop. Phool kept asking. That persistence turned a flower-recycling company into a biomaterials company. Fleather was only the start. You don't build new materials by rebranding old ones. You build them in the lab, one experiment at a time.

The entrepreneurship. Science on its own doesn't reach the market. Someone has to take the risk nobody else will underwrite, translate science into products, find customers for a material that didn't exist, and survive the long gap between proof of concept and a working business. Most good ideas die in that gap. This one didn't.

The impact. None of it began with a technology. It began with empathy for a polluted river and for the women whose livelihoods now depend on this work. That empathy never became a side project. As the science deepened, the impact widened: social, economic and environmental.

Phool grew on all three at once. This is science and society converging, driven by entrepreneurial risk-taking. #skininthegame

Watch here in Episode 2 of From What To Why Not. The power of a flower.

From 𝐀𝐡𝐦𝐞𝐝𝐚𝐛𝐚𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐆𝐮𝐣𝐚𝐫𝐚𝐭, 𝐆𝐮𝐣𝐚𝐫𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐈𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐚, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐈𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐚 𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐥𝐝, there is a lot to build.

And that is exactly what makes it exciting.
